sections.h2: Where is Petersburg, VA, and why does its history show up in property records?
sections.html:
Petersburg is an independent city 21 miles south of Richmond, at the fall line of the Appomattox River, with 33,458 residents at the 2020 census (Wikipedia).

The House of Burgesses ordered Fort Henry built in 1645, three settlements were joined as the Town of Petersburg in 1748, and an 1815 fire led to a rebuilt town that became a rail and industrial hub. By 1860 it was the second-largest city in Virginia. The 1864 to 1865 Siege of Petersburg, including the Battle of the Crater, devastated it, and parts of the battlefield are preserved as Petersburg National Battlefield.

Because Petersburg is an independent city, it has no county government above it. The city assessor values property, the Commissioner of the Revenue and Treasurer handle other taxes, and the city also runs the code office that enforces building rules. The assessor's office says it maintains roughly 15,000 parcels (Petersburg appeals page).

sections.h2: Which Petersburg offices handle real estate tax?
sections.html:
Petersburg splits real estate tax among the City Assessor, the Treasurer and Billing and Collections, and the city's own pages tell residents which to call.

Wrong assessment on a real estate billCity Assessor804-733-2333
Tax amount and whether it is paidTreasurer, City Hall, 135 N. Union St.804-733-2322
Current or delinquent balance, DMV stopBilling and Collections, 144 N. Sycamore St.804-733-2346

The city lists payment options as online, in person at the Fiscal Management Office at 144 N. Sycamore Street, a drop box at that address, or mail to P.O. Box 1271, Petersburg, VA 23804. It states a 3 percent convenience fee on credit cards and none on electronic checks (city FAQs).

sections.h2: When are Petersburg real estate taxes due?
sections.html:
Petersburg bills real estate tax quarterly, and the assessor's page lists due dates of September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30.

The page ties those dates to the Land Book. Values are set as of January 1, take effect on July 1, and cover billing from that July 1 through the next June 30. The city treasurer's FAQ confirms that payments are due quarterly. The FAQ also states a current rate of $1.22 per $100 of assessed value and says City Council sets it each year, so check your bill for the rate that applies to you.

  • September 30: first quarterly installment.
  • December 31: second installment.
  • March 30: third installment.
  • June 30: final installment.

We did not find a penalty or interest rate on the pages we opened, so we leave it out. Ask Billing and Collections for a payoff that includes any late charges before you close.

Petersburg reassesses every two years as of January 1, and it mails Change of Assessment Notices on January 28 of a reassessment year to owners whose value changed.

The assessor says all assessments are reviewed every two years even if not all change, using mass appraisal methods and the sales comparison, income and cost approaches. Appraisers work by assessment neighborhood and use the AssessPro computer-assisted mass appraisal system. They study recent sales first, and they may set aside sales that are not arm's-length, such as family transfers, foreclosures, bank sales, estate sales and other distressed sales tied to court orders or divorces.

For a seller, that means a discounted sale of a house, such as one from an estate, can be set aside when the assessor studies the market (assessment page). New construction and renovations are added when substantially complete and billed in a supplement for the part of the year they were finished.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Petersburg assessment, and by when?
sections.html:
Petersburg has three steps: an office review with the City Assessor, then the Board of Equalization, then the Circuit Court.

  • Office review: the review application is due March 1 of the assessment year, or within 30 days of the date of the change notice.
  • Board of Equalization: appeals are due April 1 of the assessment year, or within 60 days of the notice date. The board has three members, owners with real estate backgrounds appointed by the circuit court judge.
  • Circuit Court: for owners unhappy with the board or who missed earlier deadlines. The city says there is no form and the filing is typically done by an attorney.

The assessor suggests calling and speaking with an appraiser before filing, and says the review is a chance to check the recorded square footage and features of your house. A request for income and expense data that goes unanswered can keep that data out of evidence later (appeals page). Virginia law also says the board starts from a presumption that the assessor's value is correct (Va. Code 58.1-3379).

sections.h2: What tax programs and local rules affect a Petersburg owner?
sections.html:
Petersburg offers a rehabilitation credit, a damage abatement and a land use program, and it requires owners of long-vacant buildings to register them.

  • Rehabilitation credit: improvements are exempt from added tax for five years. The application must be filed before work starts, with fees of $125 for residential and $250 for commercial property.
  • Damage abatement: available if a building was unfit for use for 30 days or more and the loss cut its value by $500 or more. Apply within six months of the damage.
  • Land use: initial and annual applications are due May 1, with a $500 fee.

Under the city's vacant building registry, in Sec. 22-140 of the city code, an owner of a building continuously vacant for 12 months or more must register it with the building code official. The annual fee is $100, and the owner must describe how the building will be maintained and show a rodent abatement plan (registry page). A vacant house you plan to sell should be checked against this rule first.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Petersburg tax when the house sells?
sections.html:
The tax is paid out of the sale proceeds, because Virginia puts the real estate tax lien ahead of every other lien until it is paid.

The statute requires the purchaser, or the trustee in a foreclosure, to apply proceeds to taxes and levies, which include penalties and interest, and it says the seller's share is prorated by contract (Va. Code 58.1-3340). The deed also carries a grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of value, normally paid by the seller (Va. Code 58.1-802).

Sellers with back taxes, a vacant house, repairs they cannot fund or an inherited home often look at a direct sale. The closing agent still needs a payoff from the city, so call Billing and Collections before you sign a contract. We did not confirm deed recording details on an official page, so ask the Circuit Court clerk's office about recording.

faqs.q: How often does Petersburg reassess real estate?
faqs.a: Every two years, as of January 1. Change of Assessment Notices are mailed on January 28 of a reassessment year to owners whose value changed.

faqs.q: What are Petersburg's real estate tax due dates?
faqs.a: The assessor's page lists September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30. The treasurer's FAQ says payments are due quarterly.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Petersburg assessment?
faqs.a: An office review is due by March 1 of the assessment year or within 30 days of the notice. A Board of Equalization appeal is due by April 1 or within 60 days of the notice.

faqs.q: Do I have to register a vacant house in Petersburg?
faqs.a: Yes, if the building has been continuously vacant for 12 months or more. The city's registry charges an annual fee of $100.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Petersburg house with unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is paid from the proceeds at closing. Ask Billing and Collections at 804-733-2346 for a payoff before you set a closing date.
